extracted.intended_audience: journalists, media students, media commentators and readers interested in media ethics and the BBC/Hutton inquiry
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles for journalistic reporting—especially investigative and broadcast coverage—of government claims, intelligence matters and public-interest stories. Focuses on verification, impartiality, institutional responsibility, and minimizing harm to sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impartiality / non-partisanship
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporting should avoid appearing to have already 'made up their minds' about political figures or governments; programmes and presenters must not convey predetermined judgement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lance Price: 'I felt that John Humphrys [presenter on Today Programme], Andrew Gilligan and by implication the programme itself, had made up their minds that Tony Blair and the new Labour government were untrustworthy people and that came through to me.' Avoid framing that presumes guilt or political motivations without evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification and careful consideration of evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists must consider evidence carefully and verify claims, especially when those claims come from inside government or intelligence sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clare Short: 'What do we have to do to make these decisions more carefully and consider the evidence more carefully from inside government?' Emphasises need for rigorous vetting before publicising serious claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understanding intelligence processes and expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters covering intelligence-related stories should have or consult knowledge of how intelligence works; lack of that knowledge exposes reporting to factual challenge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panel noted complaints about Gilligan’s comments were 'aimed at his lack of knowledge about the way intelligence works.' Journalists should avoid making authoritative-sounding claims in domains they do not understand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reactive, day-to-day 'battle' reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists should not be overly focused on reacting to the government's daily agenda; they should look beyond immediate skirmishes to broader context and long-term implications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Richard Tait: journalists were 'too focused on reacting to the government’s agenda and ... the challenge is to look beyond the daily battle.' Avoid chasing daily controversies at the expense of deeper reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Holding power to account
rubrics_metrics.description: A core role of the media is to tell the truth and hold those in power accountable, scrutinising claims rather than uncritically relaying them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discussion question posed: whether the media failed to tell the British public the truth and hold power to account. Use investigative diligence and scepticism when evaluating official narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize harm to sources and individuals
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporting should consider the potential harm to named or unnamed sources and to individuals implicated in disputes; avoid reporting styles that may unduly endanger or overwhelm them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Richard Tait recounted that Kelly 'gets caught up in a knife fight between the BBC and Alastair Campbell, which he was [ill-equipped] to deal with.' Reporters should weigh public interest against foreseeable harms to people involved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional accountability and requirement for systemic correction
rubrics_metrics.description: Failures in reporting and institutional responses should prompt organisational reflection and reforms; institutions must correct systemic problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clare Short hoped Chilcot would say 'all our institutions failed and need some correcting.' Editorial processes and governance should be reviewed after major failures (e.g., Hutton) to prevent recurrence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain public trust and credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Protecting the organisation’s credibility with the public is essential; perceived honesty and reliability affect whether audiences believe reporting more than official sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Greenslade noted that 'in spite of Hutton, British people believed the BBC more than the government.' Editorial decisions should prioritise long-term trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resist echoing government spin or 'truths that suited'
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists should avoid uncritically repeating government or communications-office talking points that are selected to suit a political agenda.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panel observed the communications office tried to 'point to the truths that suited.' Be wary of accepting official framing; independently verify and challenge 'spin.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid narrowing to minute details at expense of broader context
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not become fixated on a narrow, detailed aspect of a story if that focus obscures the wider, more important context and consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Richard Tait: 'they got stuck into a very detailed aspect of the story … and at the end … you have a situation' with tragic consequences. Balance granular enquiry with contextual synthesis.
